18 March 2007 By NAME_1 NAME_2 170 Comments

    
Regular expressions are extremely powerful. This is something I read at least once or twice every day while reading articles and blogs on the Web.

While browsing today, I found this page which thoroughly describes the use of the regular expression /^1?$|^(11+?)\1+$/ in Perl to check if a number is prime or not!!!

/^1?$|^(11+?)\1+$/
To be frank, I was skeptical. The regular expression looks like magic! And I wanted to understand it better. I rewrote it in Ruby using irb and I tested it:

NAME_1@noulakaz:~$ irb

irb(main):001:0> def is_prime(n)
irb(main):002:1> (“1” * n) !~ /^1?$|^(11+?)\1+$/
irb(main):003:1> end
=> nil

irb(main):004:0> is_prime(10)
=> false

irb(main):005:0> is_prime(11)
=> true

irb(main):006:0> is_prime(12)
=> false

irb(main):007:0> is_prime(13)
=> true

irb(main):008:0> is_prime(99)
=> false

irb(main):009:0> is_prime(100)
=> false

irb(main):010:0> is_prime(101)
=> true

Great! It also works in Ruby! This means that there is no (Perl) magic going on. The regular expression really works. But how? Let’s try to follow the logic behind it.

Is 7 prime?

To know this, the function first generates “1111111” (from “1” * 7) and tries to see if that string does not match /^1?$|^(11+?)\1+$/. If there is no match, then the number is prime.

Notice that the regular expression has two parts (separated with the vertical bar |).

The first part is /^1?$/ is trivial and matches with beginning of line (^), an optional 1 (1?)
and end of line ($) which implies that it matches either the empty string or “1”. This simply indicates that calling that function with n==0 or n==1 will correctly return false (as the “1” * n will match with the first part of the regular expression)

The second part is where the magic occurs…

/^(11+?)\1+$/ matches with beginning of line (^) then by (11+?) then by \1+ and finally by end of line ($). I guess that you know that \1 is a variable which is bound to whatever was matched previously (in our case by (11+?)).

Let’s proceed slowly…

(11+?) does two things

It matches with “1” followed by one or more ones minimally. This means that it matches with “11” initially (notice that if there was no ? (i.e. (11+) was used instead, the whole string would have matched)
The string obtained (“11” initially) is bound to the variable \1.
\1+ then matches with whatever has been matched above (“11” initially) repeated one or more times. If this match succeeds then the number is not prime.

class GPT3API:
    def __init__(self, api_key: str, model_name: str):
        openai.api_key = api_key

        self.max_token_limit = 4096
        self.log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

    def truncate_text(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text[:min(len(text), self.max_token_limit)]

    def send_message(self, input_text: str, prompt: str) -> str:
        input_text = self.truncate_text(input_text)
        prompt = self.truncate_text(prompt)

        self.log.info(f"Sending message: {input_text} + {prompt}")

        retries = 0
        max_retries = 5
        delay = 1

        while retries < max_retries:
            try:
                response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
                    model=self.model_name,
                    messages=[
                        {"role": "system", "content": prompt},
                        {"role": "user", "content": input_text + " " + prompt}
                    ]
                )
                message_content = response.choices[0].message.content
                self.log.info(f"Received message: {message_content}")
                return message_content
            except openai.OpenAIError as e:
                self.log.warning(f"API Error: {e}")
                if "number of tokens exceeds" in str(e):
                    self.log.warning("Truncating text and retrying...")
                    input_text = self.truncate_text(input_text)
                    prompt = self.truncate_text(prompt)
                else:
                    self.log.warning("Retrying after a delay...")
                    time.sleep(delay)
                    retries += 1

# new stopping implementation
class KeywordsStoppingCriteria(StoppingCriteria):
    def __init__(self, keywords, tokenizer, input_ids):
        self.keywords = keywords
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.start_len = None
        self.input_ids = input_ids

    def __call__(self, output_ids: torch.LongTensor, scores: torch.FloatTensor, **kwargs) -> bool:
        if self.start_len is None:
            self.start_len = self.input_ids.shape[1]
        else:
            outputs = self.tokenizer.batch_decode(output_ids[:, self.start_len:], skip_special_tokens=True)[0]
            for keyword in self.keywords:
                if keyword in outputs:
                    return True
        return False

To see whether a consensus is reached, one needs a measure of it. Under SFP, a natural approach is to assume the system state to be a probability measure (or distribution) over the set of beliefs (referred to as the belief distribution). By introducing this notion of system states, one can quantify how much agents reach a consensus through the variance of the belief distribution. 
Intuitively, for each population,  a value of zero for the variance means that agents within that population develop exactly the same beliefs and achieve consensus.
The main challenge thereby is to analyze the evolution of the belief distribution, which requires the development of new techniques beyond the classic approach of stochastic approximation in the SFP literature.
We address this challenge by establishing a system of nonlinear partial differential equations---continuity equations---to describe the continuous-time change in the belief distribution. import game

import snake

class SnakeGameApp:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.root.title("Snake Game")
        self.root.configure(bg="black")

        self.menuFrame = tk.Frame(root, bg="black")
        self.menuFrame.pack()

        self.startButton.pack(side=tk.LEFT)

        self.restartButton = tk.Button(self.menuFrame, text="Restart Game", command=self.resetGame)

        self.difficultyButton = tk.Button(self.menuFrame, text="Change Difficulty", command=self.showChangeDifficultyDialog)
        self.difficultyButton.pack(side=tk.LEFT)

        self.pauseButton = tk.Button(self.menuFrame, text="Pause", command=self.pauseResumeGame)
        self.pauseButton.pack(side=tk.LEFT)

        self.quitButton = tk.Button(self.menuFrame, text="Quit", command=root.quit)
        self.quitButton.pack(side=tk.LEFT)

        self.difficultyLabel = tk.Label(self.menuFrame, text="Difficulty: 1", bg="black", fg="white")

        self.gameFrame.pack()

An embedding is a mapping of a discrete — categorical — variable to a vector of continuous numbers. In the context of neural networks, embeddings are low-dimensional, learned continuous vector representations of discrete variables. Neural network embeddings are useful because they can reduce the dimensionality of categorical variables and meaningfully represent categories in the transformed space.

Neural network embeddings have 3 primary purposes:

Finding nearest neighbors in the embedding space. These can be used to make recommendations based on user interests or cluster categories.
As input to a machine learning model for a supervised task.
For visualization of concepts and relations between categories.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

class DataLoader:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.root.title("Load Data and Train Model")
        self.root.geometry("500x300")
        self.window = self.root


    def load_data(self, root):
        filetypes = [("CSV files", "*.csv"), ("All files", "*.*")]
        file_path = filedialog.askopenfilename(
            title="Select a file",
            filetypes=filetypes,
            defaultextension=".csv, .txt",
            confirmfiles=False
        )
        if not file_path:
            return None

        if file_path.endswith(".txt"):
            with open(file_path, "r") as file:
                data = pd.read_csv(pd.io.txt(file.read(), header=None, delimiter=" "))
        else:
            data = pd.read_csv(file_path)
        return data

    
    def train_model(self, X, y):
        scaler = StandardScaler()
        X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X)
        X_test = scaler.transform(X)

        model = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(1,), max_iter=1000, random_state=42)
        model.fit(X_train, y)

        y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
        score = mean_squared_error(y, y_pred)
        print(f"Mean Squared Error: {score}")
        r2 = r2_score(y, y_pred)
        print(f"R^2 Score: {r2:.2f}")
